title: The plastic bag charge
issue: Has charging for plastic bags helped the environment?

title: Tourists in the old quarter
issue: Has tourism been good for a heritage district?

sources.provenance: A tourism board's annual report.
sources.text: Visitor numbers to the old quarter doubled in five years. Forty new businesses opened and 600 jobs were created.

sources.provenance: A third-generation spice shop owner, interviewed by a heritage society.
sources.text: My rent tripled. The tailor and the coffee shop beside me have gone; a souvenir shop and a bar took their place. The tourists come to see the old quarter, but the old quarter is leaving.

sources.provenance: A travel blogger's post after a one-day visit.
sources.text: The shophouses are beautifully restored and the street art is everywhere. I spent a whole day here and it felt like stepping into the past.

sources.provenance: A young resident who works as a tour guide, quoted in a newspaper.
sources.text: I earn my living walking visitors through streets my grandmother grew up in. Without the tourists these shophouses would have been pulled down years ago.

questions.question: How different are Sources A and B? Explain your answer.
questions.model: They differ on whether tourism has helped the businesses of the old quarter. A says 'forty new businesses opened'. B says the old ones are going: 'the tailor and the coffee shop beside me have gone'. They are similar in showing that tourism has brought new shops. A counts 'forty new businesses' and B names 'a souvenir shop and a bar'. They also differ in purpose. A is a tourism board's report, written to show its work as a success, so it counts only what was gained. B speaks to a heritage society and wants readers to see what is being lost.

questions.question: How useful is Source C in helping you understand whether tourism has preserved the old quarter's heritage? Explain your answer.
questions.model: It is useful. It shows the buildings have been kept: 'the shophouses are beautifully restored'. It is limited. The blogger saw the quarter for one day and judged by how it looks. Source B says the old trades are leaving — 'the tailor and the coffee shop beside me have gone'. So the buildings are preserved while the way of life is not, and C cannot see that. C is useful for the look of the quarter, not for its living heritage.

questions.question: 'Tourism has been good for the old quarter.' Using the sources, explain how far you would agree with this statement.
questions.model: Source A agrees: '600 jobs were created'. Source D agrees too: without tourists the shophouses 'would have been pulled down years ago'. Source B disagrees: 'my rent tripled' and the old shops 'have gone'. C seems to agree, but it only shows the buildings look good. A is from the tourism board, which gains from good numbers. D and B both live there, and both can be right: tourism saved the buildings and pushed out the old trades. So I agree to some extent — good for the buildings and for jobs, not for the community that made the quarter worth visiting.

title: Cats in flats
issue: Should residents be allowed to keep cats in public flats?

sources.provenance: A resident's feedback to the town council.
sources.text: The cat from the next unit walks along the corridor ledge and dirties my shoe rack. I have asked the owner three times. Rules exist for a reason.

sources.provenance: A town council officer, quoted in a newspaper.
sources.text: Most complaints we receive are about a few owners who let their cats roam. We cannot inspect every flat.

sources.provenance: An online poster by the cat welfare group, released on the day the ministry opened a public consultation on the rule.
sources.text: [The poster shows a cat behind a window, looking out.] Caption: '34 years in hiding. Tell the ministry it's time. Consultation closes 30 June.'

questions.question: What does Source C tell you about the problem with cats in flats? Explain your answer.
questions.model: The problem comes from a small number of careless owners, not from cats in general. The officer says most complaints are about 'a few owners who let their cats roam'. So it is the roaming, which the owner controls, that causes trouble.

questions.question: How reliable is Source B about whether cats can be kept responsibly in flats? Explain your answer.
questions.model: It is fairly reliable. B says that when cats were 'kept indoors', complaints 'fell from 31 a year to 9'. Source C supports this: most complaints are about owners 'who let their cats roam'. So keeping cats in does remove the main problem. But B is by a group that wants the rule changed, and it reports a pilot in 'one estate' with owners who chose to register. It is written to persuade, so the figures can be trusted more than the idea that every owner would do the same.

questions.model: It says that cat owners have been forced to hide their pets for too long. The cat is behind a window and the caption says '34 years in hiding'. The group wants people to write in to the ministry in support of changing the rule before 30 June.

title: Hiring from abroad
issue: Has hiring foreign professionals benefited local workers?

sources.provenance: The chief executive of a technology firm, speaking at a business forum.
sources.text: We hired 40 engineers from abroad because we could not find these skills here. Their projects created 150 more jobs, most of them filled by locals.

sources.provenance: A local graduate's online post.
sources.text: I sent 60 applications in a year. At my last interview the whole team had been brought in from overseas. They said I lacked experience. How do I get experience if nobody hires me?

sources.provenance: A statement by the manpower ministry.
sources.text: Firms must advertise openings to locals for 28 days before applying for a foreign work pass. Last year 300 firms were placed on a watchlist for not giving locals fair consideration.

sources.provenance: A local engineer in the same industry, interviewed by a newspaper.
sources.text: I learnt cloud systems from a colleague from abroad who sat next to me for two years. I now lead a team of twelve.

questions.question: How similar are Sources A and D? Explain your answer.
questions.model: They are similar in showing that foreign hires benefit locals. A says their projects 'created 150 more jobs, most of them filled by locals'. D says he learnt from a foreign colleague and 'now lead a team of twelve'. They differ in the kind of benefit. A is about the number of jobs. D is about skills passed on: 'I learnt cloud systems from a colleague from abroad'. They also differ in purpose. A is a chief executive defending his firm's hiring to a business audience, so he gives the numbers that make it look good. D is describing his own career and has nothing to defend.

questions.question: How useful is Source B in helping you understand whether locals are treated fairly in hiring? Explain your answer.
questions.model: It is useful. It shows some locals feel shut out: after '60 applications' he met a team 'brought in from overseas'. It is limited. It is one person's experience, and we are not told why he was turned down. Source C says '300 firms were placed on a watchlist for not giving locals fair consideration', so B's experience is not a one-off. B is written in frustration, to win sympathy, but its claim fits the official figures. It is useful as an example of a real problem, not for how common the problem is.

questions.question: 'Hiring foreign professionals has benefited local workers.' Using the sources, explain how far you would agree with this statement.
questions.model: Source A agrees: the foreign engineers' projects 'created 150 more jobs, most of them filled by locals'. Source D agrees: he learnt from a foreign colleague and now leads 'a team of twelve'. Source B disagrees: after '60 applications' he is still without a job while a whole team came 'from overseas'. Source C partly disagrees: '300 firms' were on a watchlist for unfair hiring. A has a reason to defend his own hiring, but D backs him from a worker's side with nothing to gain. B is one case, though C shows such cases exist. So I agree to a large extent: locals who get in the door benefit, but some firms do not give locals a fair chance to get in.

title: Community service hours

title: Car-free weekends
issue: Have car-free weekends improved the town centre?

sources.text: From January, the town centre's main street will be closed to cars on weekends. In the trial, footfall rose 30% and air quality improved.

sources.provenance: A resident who walks with a frame, quoted in a newspaper.

questions.question: How different are Sources B and C? Explain your answer.
questions.model: They differ on what the car-free weekends did to business. B's 'weekend sales fell by a third'. C says 'every table is full'. They are similar in showing that the scheme changed how customers reach the shops. B's customers 'cannot carry' furniture 'to a bus stop'. C's families 'stay for hours' because the street has no cars. They also differ in purpose. B writes to the agency to get the scheme changed, so he stresses his loss. C writes for neighbours and wants them to enjoy and support the car-free days.

questions.question: How useful is Source A in helping you understand the effect of car-free weekends on the town centre? Explain your answer.
questions.model: It is useful. It shows more people came: 'footfall rose 30%'. It is limited. It gives one figure for the whole street and says nothing about who lost out. Source B's 'weekend sales fell by a third', and Source D says the drop-off point is now '300 metres from the clinic'. A is the agency's notice announcing its own scheme as permanent, so it reports only the results that support the decision. It is useful for the overall crowd, not for the effect on every shop and resident.

questions.question: 'Car-free weekends have improved the town centre.' Using the sources, explain how far you would agree with this statement.
questions.model: Source A agrees: 'footfall rose 30% and air quality improved'. Source C agrees: 'every table is full' and families stay for hours. Source B disagrees: his 'weekend sales fell by a third'. Source D disagrees: the drop-off is now '300 metres from the clinic', a long way with a walking frame. A is the agency defending its own scheme, but C's full café fits its figure, so the gain is real. B and D speak only for themselves, but nothing in A or C answers them. So I agree to a large extent: the centre is livelier and cleaner for most, while shops selling large goods and people who cannot walk far are worse off.

title: A forwarded message
issue: How do false messages online affect harmony between neighbours?

sources.provenance: A message forwarded widely in an estate's chat groups one evening. The sender is not known.
sources.text: WARNING: a group of foreigners has been seen damaging cars at the Block 12 car park. Keep your children indoors. Forward to everyone.

sources.provenance: A police statement issued the next day.
sources.text: Two cars were scratched at Block 12. A 15-year-old resident has been arrested. No group was involved. The message being forwarded is false.

sources.provenance: A resident from abroad who has lived in the block for ten years, interviewed by a newspaper.
sources.text: After the message went round, my neighbour of ten years stopped greeting me in the lift. Even after the police statement, it took weeks before she spoke to me again.

sources.provenance: A poster by the estate's residents' committee, issued in the week after the police statement.
sources.text: [The poster shows a phone. The 'forward' arrow on its screen turns into a crack that runs down a corridor between two front doors.] Caption: 'One second to forward. Years to rebuild. Check before you share.'

questions.question: What does Source C tell you about the effect of the false message? Explain your answer.
questions.model: The harm lasted even after the message was shown to be false. The neighbour 'stopped greeting me in the lift', and 'even after the police statement, it took weeks before she spoke to me again'. Trust broke quickly and came back slowly.

questions.question: How reliable is Source A about what happened at Block 12? Explain your answer.
questions.model: It is not reliable. A says 'a group of foreigners' damaged cars. Source B, the police statement, says one '15-year-old resident has been arrested' and 'no group was involved'. Only the damage to cars is true. A has no named sender and tells readers to 'forward to everyone'. It is written to alarm and to spread, not to report, so it names a group to blame without any proof.

questions.question: Why was Source D issued? Explain your answer.
questions.model: It says that forwarding an unchecked message can break trust between neighbours. The forward arrow becomes a crack between two front doors. It is aimed at the residents of the estate, who had passed the false message on. It was issued in the week after the police statement. The committee wants residents to stop and 'check before you share', so that a false message does not divide the estate again.
